doc.title: Ann Rabson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 21, 2007

title: Kids writing blues lyrics and what she does with them
summary: Teachers use the A-A-B blues form; students' poems about grandparents and abuse raise questions about what to share.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: The lyric form of the blues works well for teachers, I have found out, because they can have the kids write that A-A-B form really easily and they can tell their little stories and all that. So it’s a good connection.

It’s wonderful. And I love it when schools, when I show up and the kids have written poems. Sometimes they’re so deep. I mean there was one who wrote about their grandfather dying, or their grandparents dying, and how much they missed them. And I mean it was just exquisite. It was just beautiful, a lot of feeling and I really, yeah.

When you’re in that situation — and I’ve seen you do that — there you are on the piano in front of all these kids and here’s this stack of lyrics, you know, from the third or fourth graders. When you put that in front of you, talking about their grandfather dying, do you wonder, should I share this with the school here.

Yeah. I do wonder. I do wonder. And sometimes there are ones that I don’t. In fact there are some — there have been times where I’ve talked to the teacher afterward. I mean there’s one where they’re being abused by their parents or they feel that they are. There’s a lot where they’re being abused by their siblings, and I mean I’m really into that one. I mean not sexually abused but yeah, there are ones. Mostly they’re pretty silly. And lot of them are about school. In fact, that always leads me into that song “Schoolday,” that Chuck Berry song that I do, because it’s wonderful for the kids to know that other people hated school and they wrote about it.
